strengths: The core idea is interesting and well-motivated: adapting BALD-style epistemic uncertainty estimation from active learning to inference-time noise seed selection in video diffusion, using attention maps as the stochastic predictive distribution. This is a novel, model-aware alternative to externally designed noise priors (FreeInit, FreqPrior, PYoCo, FreeNoise).

The method is practical and efficient: the Bernoulli-masked attention approximation yields multiple stochastic attention samples from a single forward pass, and the correlation-based layer truncation keeps overhead modest (+8%/+13% on CogVideoX-2B/5B).

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: large-scale testing on VBench (4,730 videos per configuration) across two model scales, plus a useful set of ablations—acquisition function comparison (random/entropy/BANSA-D/BANSA-B), ensemble size K, noise pool size M, layer truncation (Table 5), temporal scope (Table 6), and an informative reverse-selection control (Table 4).
The limitations section is honest, and the supplementary material includes a proof of the zero-condition proposition and clarification of the sign convention.
weaknesses: The reported gains are small: +0.63 total VBench on CogVideoX-2B and only +0.25 on CogVideoX-5B, with quality score improving by just +0.17 on 5B. Despite generating 4,730 videos per configuration, the paper reports no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or variance across seeds, making it hard to judge whether the 5B improvement is meaningful rather than noise.

The 'Bayesian' framing is overstated. The stochasticity is injected artificially via post-softmax Bernoulli masking rather than arising from any posterior over model parameters, and the authors themselves admit in a footnote that BANSA 'is not derived from a formal Bayesian posterior.' The theoretical grounding is thus thinner than the branding suggests, and no analysis of the bias of BANSA-E (acknowledged as biased) is provided.

There are no direct quantitative comparisons with prior noise-initialization methods (FreeInit, FreqPrior). They are dismissed as 'not officially supported on CogVideoX,' but the claim that ANSE 'reduces inference cost by approximately 64% while achieving comparable or superior generation quality' is unsupported without any head-to-head numbers. The orthogonality claim ('can be combined with these methods') is also untested.

Only two backbones are evaluated, both CogVideoX, so the generalization claim ('across various text-to-video architectures') is weakly supported. Evaluation on even one additional architecture (e.g., HunyuanVideo, Open-Sora, or Wan) would substantially strengthen the paper.

There is an internal sign inconsistency: the main paper defines BANSA as mean-of-entropies minus entropy-of-mean (Eq. 4), while the implementation uses the negated BALD-style formulation (Appendix B). Although the authors argue the ordering is preserved, this inconsistency between the main text and the actual method is confusing and suggests the formulation was retrofitted.

The mechanism connecting low attention entropy disagreement to downstream video quality is asserted empirically (correlation analysis on a small set of 100 prompts) but not analyzed; the layer-selection threshold (τ=0.7) and masking probability (p=0.2) appear as hand-tuned hyperparameters without sensitivity analysis, raising mild overfitting concerns since the correlation analysis uses the same VBench prompts later used for evaluation.

The reverse-selection control (Table 4) shows only a small degradation (82.08→81.93 vs. 82.56 for the forward direction), suggesting the BANSA score's discriminative signal, while directionally correct, is fairly weak overall.

strengths: Timely and interesting problem: inference-time noise seed selection for text-to-video diffusion is a practically relevant and underexplored angle, and framing it via attention-based uncertainty (adapting BALD to the attention space) is a reasonable conceptual idea.
Efficiency-oriented engineering is sensible: the Bernoulli-masked attention approximation reduces cost to a single denoising step and a truncated set of layers, with only ~8-13% inference overhead.

The evaluation includes several useful controls and ablations: comparison of acquisition functions (random, entropy, dropout vs. Bernoulli variants), ensemble size K, noise pool size M, layer-selection correlation analysis, temporal scope, a full-layer vs. truncated comparison, and a reversed-criterion control experiment.
The paper is generally well organized and clearly written, with quantitative results on both CogVideoX-2B and -5B and a decent number of generated videos (4,730 per configuration).
weaknesses: The headline improvements are very small (total VBench +0.63 on 2B, +0.25 on 5B) with no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance analysis over seeds. Given seed-level stochasticity, gains of this magnitude may not be meaningful, and some per-dimension changes are inconsistent across models.

Missing baselines and comparisons undermine the central claims: no quantitative comparison against FreeInit, FreqPrior, or other seed-selection/noise-optimization methods (InitNo, ReNO, 'Good Seed'), which are cited but dismissed as 'not officially supported' and 'impractical to re-implement'. The claim of '64% cost reduction while achieving comparable or superior quality' is therefore unsupported by any direct experiment.

The Bayesian grounding is weak. Bernoulli masking of attention logits is not a posterior perturbation of the model; masking logits pre-softmax introduces a systematic bias (rows with all-masked logits become uniform attention), so the 'stochastic samples' are not exchangeable draws from a meaningful uncertainty distribution. The paper itself concedes in a footnote that 'Bayesian' is used only 'in the spirit of' the method, and the sign of Eq. (4) contradicts the implementation (acknowledged only in the appendix), which is sloppy for the core formulation.

Proposition 1 is a trivial application of Jensen's inequality, and the reversed-criterion control (Table 4) actually weakens the paper: selecting the highest-uncertainty seeds yields 81.93 vs. the 82.08 vanilla baseline, i.e., barely a degradation, suggesting BANSA is only weakly informative about generation quality.

Generalizability claims are overstated: experiments cover only the CogVideoX family; no results on other T2V backbones (e.g., Open-Sora, HunyuanVideo, LTX-Video) despite the claim of being 'generalizable' and 'architecture-agnostic'.

The evaluation protocol deviates from standard practice (VBench-long with GPT-4o-augmented prompts), making the absolute numbers hard to compare against published results for either the baseline models or competing methods.

Layer selection via cumulative Pearson correlation with a fixed threshold (τ=0.7) appears tuned post hoc on the same models used for evaluation, and the correlation-vs-quality reasoning in Section 3.3/Appendix E is somewhat circular (correlating BANSA scores with the quality scores they are meant to predict, on the same 100 prompts).

Practical significance is questionable: an 8-13% inference overhead for sub-point VBench gains raises the question of whether simply sampling a few more seeds and picking via a cheap proxy would do as well; a best-of-M selection baseline using simple heuristics is not compared.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical problem: variance in video generation quality due to initial noise choice, and proposes a training-free, inference-time solution that is orthogonal to the generation process itself.

The core idea of adapting BALD-style epistemic uncertainty to the attention space of diffusion models is reasonable and clearly articulated; the Bernoulli-masked attention trick to obtain multiple stochastic attention samples from a single forward pass is a neat efficiency contribution, reducing overhead to only 8-13% inference time.
The evaluation is relatively thorough in scale: 4,730 videos per configuration on two model scales (CogVideoX-2B/5B) using the comprehensive VBench protocol.

Good ablation coverage: comparison against alternative acquisition functions (random, entropy, dropout-based), effect of ensemble size K and noise pool size M, a reversed-criterion control experiment (Table 4) that supports the causal direction of the claim, truncated vs. full-layer score comparison, and temporal scope analysis.
The paper is honest about limitations (Section 6 and the failure case in Figure 7), which is appreciated.
weaknesses: The absolute improvements are small: +0.63 total VBench score on 2B and only +0.25 on 5B. No statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or variance across repeated selection runs are reported, so it is unclear whether gains of this magnitude are robust or within noise, especially since per-seed variance is exactly the phenomenon the paper emphasizes.

No direct comparison to prior noise-prior/initialization methods (FreeInit, FreqPrior, PYoCo, FreeNoise). The justification (not officially supported on CogVideoX) is reasonable but leaves the central claim of superiority over prior art unsupported; the paper instead argues via inference cost, which is not equivalent to a quality comparison. The claim of being 'the first active noise selection framework' also overstates novelty given related seed-selection works (InitNo, Good Seed, Reno) in T2I.

There is a sign inconsistency between the main paper and appendix: Eq. (4) defines BANSA as mean-entropy minus entropy-of-mean (which is non-positive under Jensen's inequality), while the implementation uses the opposite convention. This is acknowledged only in the appendix and creates confusion about the main-paper formulation, including Proposition 1's stated direction of minimization.

The Bernoulli mask is applied to the post-softmax attention map, so masked rows no longer sum to one; the entropy of Eq. (8) is computed over non-normalized matrices, making BANSA-E a biased surrogate whose deviation from the principled BALD quantity is only acknowledged informally, not analyzed.

Generalization is demonstrated on only one model family (CogVideoX). Claims of broad applicability across 'various text-to-video architectures' are not substantiated by experiments on other backbones (e.g., HunyuanVideo, Wan, Open-Sora).

The 'Bayesian' framing is thin: the authors themselves concede (footnote 1) that BANSA is not derived from a formal Bayesian posterior, and the connection between attention-map disagreement under artificial masking and epistemic uncertainty about the seed quality is asserted rather than established theoretically.

Some details are under-specified or non-standard: evaluation uses a GPT-4o-augmented 'VBench-long' variant, and the layer-selection threshold (τ=0.7) and its correlation analysis appear circular (correlation to official quality scores computed from the same evaluation pipeline).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: initial noise seed choice demonstrably affects T2V quality, and prior frequency-prior methods ignore model-internal signals; the paper positions ANSE as a model-aware alternative.

The BALD-style adaptation to attention maps (BANSA) is sensible and elegantly simple: entropy of mean attention vs. mean entropy across Bernoulli-masked attention samples, with a clean zero-condition proposition (Jensen's inequality) and a practical single-pass approximation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: five backbones (AnimateDiff, CogVideoX-2B/5B, HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1), VBench quality/semantic scores, FVMD on MSR-VTT, a human preference study, and comparisons to FreeNoise/FreqPrior including a combined variant.

Thorough ablations: acquisition-function comparison (random/entropy/dropout vs. Bernoulli masking), ensemble size K, noise pool size M, masking probability p, layer truncation via correlation analysis, temporal scope, attention type (self vs. cross), CFG scale interaction, reversed-selection control experiment, equivalent-compute-budget comparison, and 95% confidence intervals over 10 runs.
Practical plug-and-play design with modest overhead (~9-15%) versus >100% for FreqPrior-based pipelines, and demonstrated compatibility with post-RL models (IPOC-2B).
Honest limitations section with a failure case, and analysis experiments (cross-prompt behavior, attention consistency, latent trajectory) that characterize what the selected seeds actually are.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core method is essentially BALD (2017) transplanted to attention maps with Bernoulli masking as the stochasticity source. The 'Bayesian' framing is loose—Bernoulli attention masking does not correspond to a meaningful posterior over model parameters, and the authors concede this only in a footnote. The theoretical contribution (a direct Jensen's inequality consequence) is thin.

Absolute gains are small: e.g., total VBench score improvements of ~0.4-2.4 points, and on the strongest backbones (Wan2.1, HunyuanVideo) several per-metric gains are within ~0.001-0.005, raising questions about practical significance even with reported CIs. Some confidence intervals in Tables 17-19 overlap or nearly overlap with the baseline.

Missing an important baseline: best-of-M selection using a cheap external evaluator (e.g., a VQA/reward model over M fully or partially generated candidates) is the natural competitor for the same compute budget, and would clarify how much the internal attention signal actually adds over generic candidate selection.

The prompt-dependence analysis (Experiment 1) shows seeds do not transfer across prompts, which somewhat limits the practical value proposition and suggests the method is close to best-of-M sampling with a heuristic selector; the paper could engage more critically with this.

Statistical treatment is somewhat inconsistent: main tables report averaged scores over 5 repetitions without variance, while CIs appear only in the appendix; significance of the small per-dimension gains on large models is not fully established.

Reproducibility is not yet demonstrated: code is promised ('will be made publicly available'), and several key details (e.g., which layers/attention types are used per architecture beyond the truncation depth, exact partial-NFE implementation) are deferred to appendices or future release.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on VBench, which is known to be imperfectly correlated with human perception; the user study (12 evaluators, 30 prompts per setting) is a positive addition but relatively small scale.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and practical problem: variance across initial noise seeds in text-to-video diffusion, and frames noise selection as an inference-time scaling opportunity.
The proposed acquisition function is simple, plug-and-play, and does not require retraining, which makes it easy to adopt.

Evaluation spans many backbones (AnimateDiff, CogVideoX-2B/5B, Wan2.1, HunyuanVideo, IPOC post-RL) and includes ablations (acquisition function variants, K, M, masking probability p, reversed selection), statistical CIs, and a user study.
The negative correlations between BANSA scores and quality metrics (Fig. 5b) and the reversed-selection control (Table 9) provide some support for the core claim.
The layer-truncation analysis (Appendix D/E) and equivalent-budget comparison (Appendix I) address efficiency concerns to some degree.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is a direct transplant of BALD/Houlsby mutual-information disagreement from classification into the attention-map space, plus Bernoulli masking and depth truncation. This is an engineering combination rather than a new principle, and the title's claim that the 'model already knows the best noise' oversells what is an entropy-based heuristic.

The 'Bayesian' framing is not well founded. Bernoulli masking of attention scores is a synthetic perturbation, not a posterior over model parameters, so BANSA does not measure epistemic uncertainty of the model; the paper itself concedes this in a footnote. The connection between masked-attention disagreement and seed quality is purely empirical.

Evidence of carelessness raises credibility concerns: in Table 5, the Vanilla rows for HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 are numerically identical (0.9562, 0.9656, 0.9850, 0.6276, 0.6137), and the '+Ours' rows are also identical — two different models producing identical VBench numbers to four decimal places is implausible and suggests copy-paste errors at best.

The gains are marginal relative to the added complexity and cost. CogVideoX-5B total score improves by only 0.19 points for +13% inference time; several Table 11 and Table 19 deltas are tiny and confidence intervals overlap (e.g., aesthetic and imaging quality in Table 19). The claimed quality improvement is not convincingly demonstrated on modern backbones.

Key baselines are missing. The most natural competitor — best-of-M selection using a cheap one-step denoised estimate scored by a reward/quality model (or by VBench-style proxies) — is never compared. FreeNoise and the seed-search work the authors themselves cite (Xu et al., 2025 'Good seed makes a good crop') are not empirically compared either; FreqPrior is evaluated only on AnimateDiff.

The Aesthetic Quality metric actually degrades on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 (0.6276 → 0.6268), and the equivalent-budget experiment (Table 16) is not properly matched (60 steps vs. '<60'), weakening the compute-fairness argument.

Several hyperparameters feel ad hoc and dataset-specific: the 0.7 correlation threshold for layer selection, per-model cutoff depths (d*=10–20), p=0.2 chosen from a table where the trend across p is inconsistent (Table 10 shows p=0.2 best on some metrics and near-worst on others).

The user study is small (12 evaluators, 30 prompts) and no inter-annotator statistics are reported. Minor presentation issues throughout (e.g., 'signicanse', 'proviied', inconsistent model naming) further detract from polish.

There is a tension in the analysis: the method is claimed to select 'more certain' noise, yet the seed quality is acknowledged to be prompt-dependent and low-BANSA seeds can still fail (Fig. 6), leaving unclear what precisely is being measured beyond a noisy quality proxy.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with a clean conceptual framing: transferring BALD-style uncertainty estimation from classification to attention maps in video diffusion for inference-time noise seed selection.

Evaluation is broad: results across five backbones (AnimateDiff, CogVideoX-2B/5B, Wan2.1, HunyuanVideo), plus post-RL (IPOC-2B) and large (Wan2.1 14B) settings, with VBench, FVMD, user study, and 95% confidence intervals (Appendix J).

Thoughtful ablations: acquisition function variants (random/entropy/dropout/Bernoulli), ensemble size K, noise pool size M, masking probability p, layer truncation d*, temporal scope, CFG scale, and equivalent compute budget comparisons.

The reversed-selection control experiment (Table 9) and the correlation analysis (Fig. 5b) add evidence that lower BANSA scores genuinely predict better generations, not just best-of-M sampling artifacts.
Honest limitations section (Sec. 7) with a failure case, and the method is plug-and-play with modest overhead (<15%) compared to multi-pass noise refinement baselines.
weaknesses: Data integrity concerns: In Table 5, the Vanilla rows for HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 are numerically identical across all six metrics (0.9562/0.9656/0.9850/0.6276/0.6137/0.9921 vs 0.9943), which is implausible for two different models and suggests a copy-paste error; similarly Table 19 repeats these same values. There is also a typo in Table 12 ('0\bar.9639') and typos in the text ('signicanse analysis ... provied'). These errors undermine confidence in the experimental reporting.

Limited theoretical grounding: The 'Bayesian' framing is weak. The K stochastic attention samples are generated by Bernoulli-masking a single deterministic attention map, not by any posterior over parameters; the disagreement being measured is artificially injected by the masks. The paper acknowledges this in a footnote, but the BALD/epistemic-uncertainty interpretation is therefore largely rhetorical, and it is unclear whether score differences across seeds reflect seed quality or mask-sampling noise (the paper does not state whether the same masks are shared across candidate seeds, which is a needed control).

Novelty is moderate: the core contribution is applying BALD entropy-of-mean vs. mean-of-entropy to attention maps, plus engineering approximations (single-step evaluation, layer truncation). No new formulation or analysis beyond a direct transposition of a well-known acquisition function.

Gains are small in absolute terms (e.g., CogVideoX-5B total VBench +0.19, CogVideoX-2B +0.63), and improvements on some metrics fall within reported confidence intervals (e.g., Aesthetic Quality slightly decreases on HunyuanVideo/Wan2.1; several imaging quality metrics decrease in Table 11).

Baseline comparisons are incomplete: FreqPrior/FreeInit are only evaluated on AnimateDiff; there is no comparison with other inference-time selection or reranking baselines (e.g., reward-model-based seed search under the same compute budget of 10 candidates), which would test whether attention entropy actually outperforms a generic best-of-N search with an external quality estimator.

Some analyses raise questions: Table 3 differences (Traj. Var. 52.34 vs 51.07) are tiny and unaccompanied by variance estimates; Experiment 1 (Table 1) uses only a single prompt pair, which is anecdotal evidence for the prompt-dependence claim.

Overhead is not negligible relative to the gains: +8% to +15% inference time for gains that are sometimes within noise, and the claim of 'principled' selection rests on an approximation whose connection to model uncertainty is unproven.
